extracted.intended_audience: products liability attorneys, litigators, corporate counsel, and other legal professionals interested in tort causation
extracted.subtask_description: A law-firm blog analysis comparing Liebeck v. McDonald’s and Shih v. Starbucks to illustrate how courts apply proximate cause and related causation doctrines in hot-drink product-liability cases and why similar facts can yield different outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The proximate cause inquiry examines the relationship between the defendant’s alleged conduct and the plaintiff’s injury: if the defendant’s conduct is too attenuated from the consumer’s injuries, the defendant cannot be held liable for those injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proximate cause exists when the defect in question increased the risk of harm to the consumer, and the consumer sustained injuries resulting from the increased risk. Courts generally test proximate cause by looking at whether the harm was a foreseeable result of the defect — meaning the business could reasonably have predicted the harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability / Scope of Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts test proximate cause by asking whether the harm was a foreseeable result of the defect — i.e., whether the business could reasonably have predicted the harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a harm (e.g., consumers spilling drinks) is generally foreseeable, courts ask whether the specific harm is 'within the scope of the risk' created by the defendant's conduct. In Shih the court held that losing one's balance during an 'unorthodox drinking maneuver' was not within the scope of the risk created by using a double cup and filling it to the brim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attenuation / Intervening (Unorthodox) Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's conduct may be too attenuated from the plaintiff's injury to be the proximate cause if intervening or unusual actions by the plaintiff break the causal chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will decline to impose liability where the plaintiff's own unexpected or unusual actions (e.g., removing a lid and performing an 'unorthodox drinking maneuver' that leads to loss of balance) are the immediate cause of injury and were not a foreseeable result of the alleged defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product/Manufacturing Defect Requires Proof of Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff alleging a manufacturing (or other product) defect must show the product was defective and that the defect proximately caused the injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shih alleged the double-cup without a sleeve and a cup filled to the brim constituted a manufacturing defect, but the court granted summary judgment because those alleged defects were held not to proximately cause her burns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Corporate Practices and Prior Incident Reports as Evidence of Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of corporate practices and prior incident reports can help establish that a product or practice increased the risk of harm and that the harm was foreseeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Liebeck, attorneys offered evidence McDonald’s instructed franchisees to brew coffee at 180–190°F and had more than 700 reports of burns; such evidence supports a finding the product was defectively dangerous and that injuries were foreseeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary Judgment When Causation Is Not Established
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plaintiff cannot prove proximate causation, the defendant can obtain summary judgment disposing of the claim without trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Shih, Starbucks moved for and obtained summary judgment on the ground that Shih could not prove proximate cause; the court agreed and the appeals court affirmed, illustrating that causation failure can be dispositive pre-trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative Fault and Damages Reduction (Remittitur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocation of fault to the plaintiff can reduce both compensatory and punitive damages awarded by a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Liebeck the jury found Liebeck 20% at fault; the court significantly reduced the punitive award, resulting in lower compensatory and punitive amounts after adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied Warranty Claims as Alternative Theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs may assert implied warranty claims (merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose) alongside defect claims in hot-drink cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liebeck alleged the coffee 'violated the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose' in addition to defect claims; while the page does not list warranty elements, it signals plaintiffs often plead multiple overlapping theories that still require proof of defect and causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Policy Role of Proximate Cause in Limiting Business Liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts use proximate cause and related doctrines to limit exposure of businesses to claims for unforeseeable consumer injuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that 25 years after Liebeck, the doctrine of proximate cause continues to serve as a public-policy limitation protecting businesses from liability for unforeseeable injuries related to hot drinks.
